questions.stem: What is an AWS Availability Zone?

options.text: One or more isolated data centers within a Region
options.rationale: Each AZ has independent power, networking and connectivity, and sits in a Region with other AZs.

options.text: A geographic area that contains several AWS Regions
options.rationale: It is the other way around: a Region contains several AZs.

options.text: A location that caches content for Amazon CloudFront
options.rationale: That describes an edge location.

options.text: A single rack of servers inside a data center
options.rationale: An AZ is far larger than a rack.

questions.explanation: Regions contain multiple, isolated Availability Zones; edge locations are separate sites used for caching and edge services.

questions.stem: Which statement about AWS Regions is correct?

options.text: Each Region contains exactly one data center
options.rationale: Regions contain multiple Availability Zones, each with one or more data centers.

options.text: Each Region is a separate area with multiple Availability Zones
options.rationale: Regions are physical locations around the world, each made up of multiple isolated AZs.

options.text: Resources are copied to every Region automatically
options.rationale: Data stays in the Region you choose unless you replicate it.

options.text: Regions and edge locations are the same thing
options.rationale: Edge locations are separate sites used to serve content.

questions.explanation: Data does not leave a Region unless you move it, which matters for data sovereignty.

questions.stem: Why should a company deploy its application across multiple Availability Zones?

options.text: To reduce network latency for customers located on other continents
options.rationale: Serving distant users is a reason to use more Regions or edge services.

options.text: To meet laws that require data to stay in one country
options.rationale: Data residency is handled by choosing the Region.

options.text: So the application stays available if one Availability Zone fails
options.rationale: AZs do not share single points of failure, so a multi-AZ design survives the loss of one.

options.text: To get a lower hourly price for Amazon EC2
options.rationale: Spreading across AZs does not reduce instance prices.

questions.explanation: High availability within a Region comes from using more than one Availability Zone.

questions.stem: A company's application must keep running even if an entire AWS Region becomes unavailable. What should the company do?

options.text: Add more instances in the same Availability Zone
options.rationale: Instances in one AZ fail together with that AZ and its Region.

options.text: Move to a larger instance type
options.rationale: Instance size does not protect against a Regional outage.

options.text: Enable MFA on the root user
options.rationale: MFA improves account security, not availability.

options.text: Deploy the workload in a second Region as part of a disaster recovery plan
options.rationale: Multi-Region designs protect against the loss of a whole Region.

questions.explanation: Reasons to use multiple Regions: disaster recovery and business continuity, low latency for distant users, and data sovereignty.

questions.stem: A company must keep customer data inside a specific country to comply with local laws. What should it consider when deciding where to deploy?

options.text: Choose an AWS Region located in that country
options.rationale: Data stays in the Region where you store it, so the Region's location addresses data residency.

options.text: Choose the Region with the lowest prices
options.rationale: Price does not satisfy legal residency requirements.

options.text: Store the data at edge locations
options.rationale: Edge locations cache content; they are not where you keep primary data.

options.text: Use any Region as long as an IAM password policy is set
options.rationale: Password policies do not control where data is stored.

questions.explanation: Data sovereignty is one of the main reasons to choose a particular Region.

questions.stem: What are AWS edge locations primarily used for?

options.text: Running Amazon RDS database instances
options.rationale: Databases run in Regions and Availability Zones.

options.text: Caching content closer to users through services such as Amazon CloudFront
options.rationale: Edge locations serve cached content and run edge services with low latency.

options.text: Grouping several AWS Regions together
options.rationale: Edge locations do not group Regions.

options.text: Storing AWS Backup vaults for long-term retention
options.rationale: Backup vaults live in Regions.

questions.explanation: CloudFront and Route 53 use edge locations to bring content and DNS answers closer to users.

questions.stem: Which service improves the availability and performance of applications by routing user traffic over the AWS global network to the nearest healthy endpoint using static IP addresses?

options.text: Amazon CloudFront
options.rationale: CloudFront caches content at edge locations; it does not provide static IP addresses for your application.

options.text: Elastic Load Balancing
options.rationale: Elastic Load Balancing distributes traffic to targets within a Region rather than routing users across the AWS global network.

options.text: AWS Global Accelerator
options.rationale: Global Accelerator provides static anycast IP addresses and routes traffic over the AWS network.

options.text: AWS Direct Connect
options.rationale: Direct Connect links an on-premises network to AWS.

questions.explanation: CloudFront speeds up content delivery with caching; Global Accelerator speeds up and stabilizes TCP and UDP traffic to applications.

questions.stem: A company wants to run latency-sensitive applications, such as real-time video rendering, close to users in a large city that is far from the nearest AWS Region. Which option should it consider?

options.text: AWS Wavelength Zones
options.rationale: Wavelength is for applications on 5G mobile networks, inside telecommunications providers' networks.

options.text: An Availability Zone in a distant Region
options.rationale: A distant Region does not provide low latency to that city.

options.text: Edge locations alone
options.rationale: Edge locations cache content but do not run general application compute.

options.text: AWS Local Zones
options.rationale: Local Zones place compute, storage and other services close to large population centers for single-digit millisecond latency.

questions.explanation: Local Zones extend a Region to a metro area. Wavelength Zones extend AWS into 5G networks.

questions.stem: Which option embeds AWS compute and storage inside telecommunications providers' 5G networks for ultra-low-latency mobile applications?

options.text: AWS Wavelength Zones
options.rationale: Wavelength Zones put AWS infrastructure at the edge of 5G networks.

options.text: AWS Local Zones
options.rationale: Local Zones serve metro areas but are not inside carrier 5G networks.

options.text: Availability Zones
options.rationale: AZs are part of a Region, not inside carrier networks.

options.text: Edge locations
options.rationale: Edge locations cache content for services such as CloudFront.

questions.explanation: Wavelength lets mobile application traffic reach AWS compute without leaving the carrier network.

questions.stem: Which TWO statements about Availability Zones are correct? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: They are the same as edge locations
options.rationale: Edge locations are separate sites for caching and edge services.

options.text: They are connected by low-latency, high-bandwidth networking
options.rationale: Fast links between AZs make synchronous replication practical.

options.text: Each Availability Zone is in a different country
options.rationale: AZs in a Region are in the same geographic area.

options.text: They are physically separated from each other within a Region
options.rationale: Separation means a local event such as a fire or flood does not affect other AZs.

options.text: They share a single power source to reduce costs
options.rationale: Each AZ has independent, redundant power.

questions.explanation: Availability Zones do not share single points of failure, which is why multi-AZ designs are highly available.
